newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Blame other guy is focus of Russian budget debate.
newsitem.headline: Blame other guy is focus of Russian budget debate.

text.p: As some deputies tell it, the Russian parliament is one big political game, with a simple rule: tar the other guy, keep your hands clean.
Wednesday's debate on cutting the 1997 budget was a prime example. Because of a shortfall in tax revenues, Russia cannot afford the budget the parliament passed earlier this year.
Short of miraculously finding new revenues, the only solution is to cut spending. But no one wants to take the blame.
"Whether or not the Duma accepts a measure on cutting spending is not of prime importance," said deputy Viktor Gitin of the liberal Yakloko group. "It's all a big game."

For the Communists, the biggest group in the Duma lower house, the government's shortfall offers a chance to revive criticism of liberal First Deputy Prime Ministers Boris Nemtsov and Anatoly Chubais and of President Boris Yeltsin.

"The government is made up of people personally responsible for policies hostile to the people -- impoverishment and rip-off privatisation. We must propose that the president review the cabinet," party leader Gennady Zyuganov told deputies.

But when Yabloko head Grigory Yavlinsky told the Duma he had collected 93 signatures calling for a vote of no-confidence in Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin's government -- an idea Zyuganov's camp might be expected to favour -- the Communists were opposed.

"I'm categorically against changing the government," Yevgeny Maximov, a communist deputy, told Reuters. "In the place of Nemtsov, Chubais and Chernomyrdin will come Yavlinsky, Gaidar and Burbulis and the same policies will start anew."
He referred to former premier Yegor Gaidar, who launched Russia's economic reforms in 1991, and former Yeltsin confidant Gennady Burbulis, both of whom are hated by Communists.
Yabloko members admit their move against Chernomyrdin's government is aimed at promoting more active reformers like Chubais or Nemtsov, an outcome abhorrent to the Communists.

Zyuganov told the Duma he had a different plan to put pressure on the government -- gathering signatures across the country demanding Yeltsin's resignation. But petitions, even if organisers gather millions of signatures, have no legal force.
Such moves do, however, give the communists the appearance of action, while at the same time they have made few concrete proposals on solving the budget crisis.
"That's the curse of Russia; everyone talks, but nothing is done," said communist deputy Maximov.
Some analysts and liberal deputies say communists and the nationalist Liberal Democrats of Vladimir Zhirinovsky have little interest in advancing useful concrete policies overall.
"For the Communist Party and the Liberal Democrats, the idea is that the worse things are in the country, the better things will be for them," said Yabloko member Gitin.
"They will criticise but not do anything."

Although Chernomyrdin told parliament he accepted blame for the shortfall in revenue, the government wants to share the responsibility for cutting spending with the Duma, which is far weaker than the executive branch under the constitution.
"Chubais wants the Duma to share the responsibility on cutting spending, as it shared the responsibility on approving the budget," Gitin said.
But even the pro-government Our Home is Russia group is resisting sharing the blame. That gave rise to a proposal to allow the government to cut spending without Duma assent.
"The government itself should face responsibility for its inability to fulfil the budget," Roman Popkovich, deputy head of Our Home, told Reuters. Our Home was founded by Chernomyrdin.
The Duma vote on the 1997 spending cuts is due on Friday.
